heading: Fintech Questions, Answered
intro: Straight answers on banking through apps, payment app balances, robo-advisers and buy now, pay later loans. They draw on FDIC, CFPB and FINRA guidance.
Read the short answer under each question. Open it for the rules, the risks, and what to check before you sign up.

topics.name: Digital Banking and Apps
topics.intro: How deposit insurance works when you bank through a technology company instead of directly with a bank.

a: The FDIC describes fintechs as technology companies that provide financial services, often online or through mobile apps. Some partner with banks; others do not.
Whether a bank is involved, and how, decides whether your money can be covered by deposit insurance. Read the app's terms to find out.

questions.q: Is money in a fintech app FDIC insured?
a: It depends. The FDIC says nonbank companies themselves are never FDIC insured. Your funds become eligible only after the company deposits them at an FDIC-insured bank and other conditions are met.
Even then, insurance covers the failure of the bank, not the failure of the app company. The FDIC notes that recovering money from a failed nonbank may take time through a bankruptcy process.
When a company places customer money at a bank in one account, coverage can pass through to each customer. The FDIC says records must identify who owns the money and how much each person owns.
If those conditions are not met, coverage may not reach individual customers as expected. Check which bank holds your money and how the app describes its coverage.

questions.q: Is a neobank the same as a bank?
a: Not necessarily. Many app-based financial companies that call themselves neobanks are not banks; they partner with chartered banks to hold deposits.
The FDIC's crypto fact sheet lists neobanks among the nonbank entities whose failure FDIC insurance does not cover. Look up the partner bank to confirm where your deposits sit.

questions.q: How do I check which bank holds my money?
a: The FDIC advises identifying the specific FDIC-insured bank or banks where an app says it will deposit your funds, then confirming that bank is insured.
The app's disclosures or terms of service usually name the partner bank. If they do not, ask the company before keeping a large balance there.

topics.name: Payment Apps
topics.intro: What happens to money you leave in a peer-to-peer payment app, and how to keep it protected.

questions.q: Is the money I keep in a payment app safe?
a: The CFPB says FDIC insurance generally does not apply to money sitting in a payment app unless you have signed up for additional services from the app.
If the app company fails and your balance is not insured, the CFPB warns you might not get your money back, or not in the guaranteed way a bank failure allows.

questions.q: How can I protect money I receive in a payment app?
a: The CFPB suggests a simple step: move money you receive out of the app promptly and into an insured bank, credit union or card account.
Use the app to send and receive, not to store. That keeps your balance in an account covered by FDIC or NCUA insurance.

questions.q: Do some payment apps offer FDIC insurance on balances?
a: Some do, with conditions. The CFPB says certain apps require you to sign up for direct deposit, register the account, use the app's own card or take another step before a balance is insured.
Coverage rules differ by app. Review your app's terms to see exactly what triggers insurance and which bank holds the funds.

questions.q: How is a payment app different from a wire transfer?
a: A payment app is a consumer service run by a company, usually linked to your bank or card. A wire is a bank-to-bank transfer, often over the Federal Reserve's Fedwire service.

Wires are generally final once processed. The guides to [what a wire transfer is](/payments/what-is-a-wire-transfer/) and [ACH vs wire transfers](/payments/ach-vs-wire-transfer/) explain the differences.

topics.name: Robo-Advisers and BNPL
topics.intro: Automated investing services and short-term installment loans offered through apps and checkout pages.

a: FINRA describes robo-advisers as services that use an algorithm to build and manage a portfolio based on an online assessment of your goals, risk tolerance, time horizon and finances.
Robo-advisers typically cost less than full-service advisers but may offer less personal support. Some firms offer hybrid services with access to a human adviser.

questions.q: Should I choose a robo-adviser or a human adviser?
a: It depends on the help you want. FINRA suggests weighing the level of service, the investments offered and the fees, which vary by firm and account type.
A simple goal, such as investing a set amount each month in a diversified portfolio, may suit automation. Complex tax or estate questions often call for a person.

questions.q: What is a buy now, pay later loan?
a: The CFPB describes BNPL as an installment loan that lets you buy something now with little or no upfront payment and pay the rest in four or fewer payments.
A common plan splits the cost into four interest-free payments every two weeks. Unlike a credit card, your creditworthiness may be checked each time you use one.

questions.q: Do buy now, pay later loans charge fees?
a: Many BNPL loans charge no interest, but the CFPB notes most do charge late fees for missed payments.
Before agreeing, check the loan documents for fees and make sure you can afford each payment on its due date. Several BNPL loans at once can be hard to track.
FINRA describes a DAO as a collectively owned organization that runs on a blockchain, with governance and decisions automated and enforced by software.
Token holders often vote on proposals, but voting power can be concentrated. The guide to [DAO governance and DeFi](/fintech/dao-governance/) explains what token voting controls.
